title: Visakha's riddles
hookLine: a later story: Visakha keeps her father's ten puzzling rules, such as "don't carry the inside fire outside"

cards: A wedding morning. A young woman named Visakha is leaving her father's house for her husband's family in another town. Her father, Dhananjaya, takes her aside with advice, and it comes as riddles.
Don't carry the inside fire outside. Don't bring the outside fire in. Give to those who give.
Don't give to those who don't. Give to both. Sit happily, eat happily, sleep happily.
Tend the fire. Honor the household gods. Her new father-in-law, Migara, overhears, baffled.

teach.b: First, the trial. Some time later, the story says, Migara turns against his daughter-in-law and wants her sent home.
She asks that her case be heard by elders who came with her from her father's town, and Migara brings up the riddles as proof that she's strange. Second, the fire.

She explains each one. The inside fire is the household's private troubles: don't carry tales of your in-laws' faults to the neighbors. The outside fire is the neighbors' quarrels and gossip: don't bring them home.
Give to those who give: lend to people who return what they borrow; and not to those who don't. Give to both: help poor relatives, repay or not.

Sitting, eating and sleeping happily mean honoring the elders of the house, and tending the fire means treating them with care, like a flame. Honoring the household gods means caring for holy people who come to the door.
The elders find her blameless. In the commentary, Migara later comes to the Buddha's teaching through her, and tradition says he honored her by calling her his mother. Fourth, what travels.
Some riddles are a young wife's duties of their own time.

But the first one travels well. A quarrel at home grows when it's carried out; a quarrel next door grows when it's carried in. Visakha kept her father's riddles until the day she could say what they meant.

how: Visakha's story is told in Theravada countries from the Dhammapada commentary, and she is remembered by the name Migaramata, 'Migara's mother', the name her father-in-law gave her.

o: a set of laws for a king's court
a game played at a wedding feast
a father's advice, given in puzzles

s: the inside fire riddle was about not lending the neighbors a light
that's what Migara thought. Visakha explains it means not carrying household troubles outside.
the story comes from the Dhammapada commentary
it's a later story, told in the commentary, not in the suttas.
she explained each riddle and was found blameless.

games.q: you're Visakha. your father-in-law has called elders to judge you, and holds up your father's riddles as proof you're strange. what do you do?
o: apologize, and promise to forget the riddles.
go home to your father's house.
games.why: she explains every riddle, the inside fire first, and is found blameless. tradition says Migara later called her his mother.

practice: Think of something about your family or a close friend that isn't yours to tell: a quarrel, a worry, an embarrassment. Not a secret that hides harm; that kind may need telling to someone who can help.
Notice the pull to share it, and let it stay inside, the way a hearth fire stays in the hearth.

wordCard.voice: Visakha's riddles. A father's puzzling advice to his daughter, and her clear explanation of each riddle when she was put on trial. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali aggi, fire: the inside fire and the outside fire of the riddles.

carryVoice: Your line: don't carry the fire out. The week's lines: she survived, from grief to teacher, she taught him, after the seed, never too late, the mango grove. See you tomorrow.
